Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy prices and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy.
Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.

Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before.

Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher energy prices brought about by the Iran war. Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports.

October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 75% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan."The BOJ is likely to look through the temporary weakness in 3Q GDP and focus instead on underlying inflation and wage dynamics," Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research, wrote in a Monday note.

news.title: Japan CPI misses on all three measures, but core stays above 2% ahead of a BoJ hike call
body: The misses take a little edge off December hike pricing, but not enough to change the base case after Ueda’s hawkish remarks on Thursday. A slower underlying gauge leaves the yen with less support than it needed near 160, so the burden falls on intervention warnings rather than rate expectations. JGB yields may ease at the front end, but producer prices running at 7.1% keep the inflation pipeline full. With energy a key driver, oil remains a swing factor for whether underlying inflation turns back up as some economists expect.
Japan’s inflation missed forecasts across the board but stayed above target, leaving the BoJ’s December hike intact and the yen still looking for support near 160.

Japan’s core inflation rate picked up in October and stayed above the Bank of Japan’s 2% target for a second straight month, although every major measure came in below forecasts. The result does little to change expectations that the BoJ will raise rates at its December meeting.

The core consumer price index, which excludes fresh food, rose 2.2% from a year earlier, below the median forecast of 2.3% but up from 2.1% in September. Headline inflation rose to 2.3% from 2.1%, short of the 2.5% expected. The index that excludes both fresh food and fuel, which the BoJ watches as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressure, slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, against a forecast of 2.3%.

That last reading is the one that gives doves something to point to. A slowdown in underlying inflation would normally argue for patience. But the gauge is still above target, and some economists expect it to accelerate sharply in the coming months as companies continue to pass on rising raw material costs. One research house now expects the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 2.5% by the middle of next year, well beyond current market pricing.

Cost pressures in the pipeline support that view. Japan’s producer prices rose 7.1% year on year in October, ahead of forecasts. Oil, chemicals, steel and utilities drove the rise, and a weak yen lifted import costs. Energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict have been a major driver of the pickup in consumer prices this year.

The BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25% after hikes in June and September, a faster pace than its roughly twice-yearly moves in 2024 and 2025. It held rates steady in October. A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be the third increase this year. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative. He also flagged an upside risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the target.

There are offsetting concerns. The economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter, and the yen is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention this year. With the Fed also hiking, a December BoJ move may do little to narrow the rate gap that has kept pressure on the yen.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: Gold slides toward $3,600 as sellers press on, but UBS upgrades it and still sees $5,000
body: UBS’s upgrade gives longer-term buyers a reason to look at gold at these levels. But the near-term flow still belongs to rates, and nothing in the call changes the picture before the December 9 Fed decision. The low $3,600s are now being tested, and a clean break would leave the market with little obvious support until the high $3,500s. A short-covering bounce is possible if US data soften or the dollar pauses, but rallies are likely to meet selling while three-hike forecasts keep spreading.
Gold keeps falling on Fed hike bets, while UBS says the wait for a recovery is getting longer but the case for owning it at these prices is getting stronger.

Gold is under heavy selling pressure again, slipping to around $3,606 an ounce in Asian trade and extending a slide that has taken it roughly 35% below its January record. The pressure is coming from the same place as all year: expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep raising rates. J.P. Morgan became the latest major bank on Thursday to forecast hikes in December, January and March. Treasury yields above 5% and a firm dollar continue to raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no income.

Against that backdrop, UBS has moved the other way. In its Year Ahead 2027 outlook, titled “Sustaining resilience,” the bank has upgraded gold to Attractive. It argues that structural demand and an eventual easing in real yields should support a recovery toward $5,000 an ounce by December 2027, which would be a gain of close to 40% from current levels.

The upgrade is part of a broader shift in UBS’s asset allocation. The bank now sees the most favourable risk-reward in bonds and commodities, followed by equities, with cash its least preferred asset class, and it has downgraded global equities to Neutral. It describes commodities as a way to protect portfolios against geopolitical disruption, inflation and constrained supply, with gold at the centre of that view.

UBS’s path to $5,000 has lengthened as the Fed has turned more hawkish. In August, the bank expected gold to reach $5,000 in the first half of 2027. As recently as October, its chief investment office saw $5,400 by September 2027. Earlier this week it pushed the $5,000 level back to the final quarter of 2027. The new outlook keeps that target but adds conviction through the upgrade. In effect, UBS is arguing that the wait may be longer, but the case is stronger at today’s prices.

The key condition is real yields. UBS expects easing inflation to allow bond yields to decline modestly later in 2027, and its chief investment office has forecast Fed hikes in December and March before that relief arrives. That sequencing explains the gap between the price and the forecast. Until real yields turn, the structural buyers UBS is counting on, chiefly central banks, are more likely to slow gold’s decline than reverse it.

Elsewhere in commodities, UBS expects oil to remain supported in the first half of 2027 and names copper as its preferred industrial metal, citing demand from electrification, power networks, data centres and AI infrastructure.

The call puts UBS among the more constructive major banks on gold, alongside Morgan Stanley at $5,250 for the fourth quarter of 2027 and ahead of Goldman Sachs at $4,650 for the end of next year. All three see higher prices from here. None sees a quick turn while the Fed is still hiking.

news.title: Fed's Paulson keeps quiet on December, says October’s pause was never meant as a stop
body: With no fresh policy signal, the speech is unlikely to move rate pricing, and a quarter-point December hike remains the strong favourite. Her “pause was not a stop” framing supports the view that the hiking cycle runs into 2027, which keeps front-end Treasury yields and the dollar supported. Her three triggers for faster hikes give traders a checklist for the 4 December payrolls report and other data before the meeting: inflation expectations, wage growth and underlying inflation. An upside surprise on wages or expectations would strengthen the case for the larger move that Waller has floated.
Paulson argues the Fed should need to say less if markets understand it, and her policy view hasn’t changed: gradual hikes, with three clear reasons to go faster.

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson stayed away from any near-term guidance on interest rates on Thursday. In a speech in New York, she argued that the Fed communicates best when the public understands how it thinks, not when officials spell out what comes next. With no fresh steer ahead of the December 8 to 9 meeting, her policy views from earlier this month remain the best guide to how she is likely to vote.

Speaking to the Money Marketeers of New York University, Paulson said understanding matters more than the particular ways the Fed communicates. If markets grasp the Fed’s reaction function, she argued, officials need to say less each time new data arrive, and policy can stay steady and largely predictable. She said the value of rate-path guidance depends on circumstances and is less useful in normal times, though Fed communications should still be clear about officials’ views.

She pointed to October as an example. The Fed held rates steady after hiking in September, but markets still expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind. In her words, shared understanding allowed policy to move deliberately, “without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop.” That was the closest she came to a signal: the October hold was a breather, not the end of the cycle.

Her remarks fit a wider debate inside the Fed. Under Chair Kevin Warsh, the central bank has shortened its policy statement and set up a task force on communications. Warsh himself has largely stepped back from giving rate guidance, even as many other officials continue to share their views.

Paulson had already shared hers. In a speech on November 10, she said policy needs to be somewhat restrictive to return inflation to 2% and that further gradual rate hikes seemed appropriate. She judged underlying inflation to be stuck between 2.5% and 3%. She also named three developments that would lead her to favour moving faster: inflation expectations drifting higher, wage pressures building, or underlying inflation rising. At the same time, she flagged that recent swings in stocks and oil could make consumer spending less durable than expected, one reason she prefers a gradual pace.

Read together, the two speeches point the same way. Paulson is a voter this year, and nothing in either speech suggests she would resist the quarter-point hike in December that markets widely expect, which would lift the target range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Thursday’s message adds that a slower pace should not be mistaken for a softer resolve.

Bitcoin hits lowest since July as Fed hike talk and a Wall Street rout collide
body: The rates message (like this: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) is hitting the whole crypto complex, not just Bitcoin. Ether dropped below $1,800 and sentiment gauges sit at extremes. Spot ETF products traded lower with the underlying, and IBIT and FBTC each fell less than 1% on the day. That leaves crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR, and listed miners, exposed to both falling token prices and a weaker tech tape. Bitcoin is trading as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge, so equity volatility and Fed pricing remain the main drivers for now.
Bitcoin is trading like a leveraged bet on Fed policy, and Thursday’s mix of hawkish minutes and a stock market rout pushed it to a four-month low.

Bitcoin fell to around $61,600 on Thursday, its lowest level since early July. The move came as a 1,000-point drop in the Dow and fresh talk of tighter Federal Reserve policy pushed investors out of riskier assets. The token was down a little over 2% on the day by early evening in New York, leaving it within reach of the $60,000 mark and roughly half its record high.

The selling tracked Wall Street closely. Bitcoin traded near $63,900 at the US open and slipped to around $62,250 by lunchtime, while the Dow shed more than 1,000 points and the VIX volatility gauge climbed above 28. A short-seller report on AMD added to pressure on tech stocks. Ether dropped below $1,800, and the widely watched Fear and Greed Index sat at 10, deep in extreme fear territory.

Rates are the bigger backdrop. Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed most officials favour further increases, with some open to a half-point move in December. The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4% in October, with two dissenters preferring a quarter-point hike. Since then, a hotter-than-expected October inflation report has met the threshold Governor Christopher Waller had set out for when a 50 basis point increase might be warranted.

Higher rates raise the cost of holding assets that pay no yield, and Bitcoin has been absorbing that message for weeks. It is on course for a seventh straight weekly loss, a run that has taken it from about $87,500 in early October.

Flows offer little support. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw more than $300 million in net outflows on Wednesday, taking November’s total to roughly $2.6 billion, and analysts also point to miners selling into a thinning market.

Traders will watch whether the $60,000 level holds, Thursday’s ETF flow data for any sign that redemptions are slowing, and incoming US data ahead of the Fed’s December meeting. A run of softer numbers could cool hike expectations quickly. Another hot print would likely keep the pressure on.
